title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
subtitle: The directions a matrix only stretches
subject: Linear algebra

slides.title: Eigenvalues and **eigenvectors**
slides.subtitle: The directions a matrix only stretches, and why they make hard problems easy

slides.title: After this lesson you can
points: decide whether a vector is an eigenvector of a matrix
find the eigenvalues of a $2\times2$ matrix from its characteristic equation
check your result with the trace and the determinant

slides.title: Some directions are special for a matrix

points.text: Most vectors change **direction** when you multiply by $A$. A few special ones do not.
points.detail: Think of $A$ as a machine that stretches and turns the plane. Along some lines it only stretches.

points.text: Along those directions $A$ acts like a number: $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v$.
points.detail: A whole matrix collapses to one scalar $\lambda$, which is far easier to compute with.

points.text: Knowing them turns $A^{100}$, differential equations and Markov chains into scalar problems.
points.detail: If $A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v$ then $A^{100}\mathbf v = \lambda^{100}\mathbf v$: no hundred multiplications needed.

points.text: They are behind PCA, vibration modes, PageRank and stability analysis.
points.detail: These are the applications the lecture names; the rest of this lesson builds the tool they all share.

slides.lead: Multiply a vector by a matrix and it usually changes direction. The few vectors that do not are the key to understanding what the matrix does.
slides.explain: The idea of this whole chapter is to look for the directions a matrix does not rotate. Once you have them, you can describe $A$ by how much it stretches along each one, and every later computation gets simpler.
slides.takeaway: An eigenvector is a direction that $A$ only stretches; the stretch factor is the eigenvalue.

slides.definition: Let $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$. A vector $\mathbf v \neq \mathbf 0$ with $$A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v$$ is an **eigenvector** of $A$, and the scalar $\lambda$ is its **eigenvalue**.
slides.example: For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf e_1$ is an eigenvector with $\lambda = 2$ and $\mathbf e_2$ one with $\lambda = 3$.
slides.explain: Read $A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v$ aloud: applying $A$ to $\mathbf v$ gives the same vector again, only multiplied by a number. That number is $\lambda$. The vector must not be $\mathbf 0$, because the zero vector satisfies the equation for every $\lambda$ and would make the definition empty.
slides.intuition: Picture stretching a rubber sheet horizontally. A horizontal arrow drawn on it just gets longer. An arrow at an angle changes its angle as well.

captions: A typical vector $\mathbf w = (1, 0)$ is sent to $(2, 1)$: its direction **changes**.
But $\mathbf v = (1, 1)$ goes to $(3, 3) = 3\mathbf v$. Same line, stretched by $\lambda = 3$.
These two lines, the **eigenspaces**, are the directions $A$ only scales.
slides.lead: The matrix $A$ below acts on the plane. Follow one ordinary vector and then the two special ones.
slides.explain: The first arrow is turned: its direction after multiplication differs from before. The arrow along $(1,1)$ stays on its own line and becomes three times as long, so $\lambda = 3$. The arrow along $(1,-1)$ stays exactly as it was, so $\lambda = 1$. The two dotted lines are the only directions $A$ keeps.
slides.takeaway: Look for vectors whose image lies on the same line as the vector itself.

slides.title: Finding eigenvalues

steps.why: subtract $\lambda\mathbf v$ from both sides and factor out $\mathbf v$

steps.text: A non-zero solution exists exactly when $A - \lambda I$ is singular
steps.why: a non-zero solution exists only when the matrix is singular, and singular means determinant $0$

steps.text: For our matrix, expand the determinant

slides.lead: We want every $\lambda$ for which the equation $A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v$ has a solution other than $\mathbf 0$.
slides.explain: The trick is the third line: instead of searching for a vector, we ask when a non-trivial solution can exist at all. That turns a search over infinitely many vectors into one equation in the single unknown $\lambda$.

slides.title: Finding an eigenvector for $\lambda = 3$

steps.why: we put the value of $\lambda$ into $A - \lambda I$
two equations that say the same thing, so only one condition remains
any non-zero multiple is again an eigenvector

slides.lead: With $\lambda = 3$ known, the eigenvectors are the non-zero solutions of one linear system.
slides.explain: Eigenvectors are only determined up to a scale factor. That is why the answer is a whole line of vectors, written with a free parameter $t$, and not a single vector.

slides.question: A matrix $A$ is singular. Which number is certainly an eigenvalue?
slides.explain: Singular means $A\mathbf v = \mathbf 0 = 0\cdot\mathbf v$ for some $\mathbf v \neq \mathbf 0$, so $\lambda = 0$. The trace is the *sum* of the eigenvalues, not one of them.

slides.title: Two checks that save work

points.detail: Add the eigenvalues and you get the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$.
Multiply them and you get the determinant.

points.text: Triangular matrix: the eigenvalues are the **diagonal entries**.
points.detail: No determinant is needed: read the eigenvalues off the diagonal.

points.text: Real symmetric matrix: real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.
points.detail: Symmetry guarantees real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvector directions.

slides.lead: Once you have the eigenvalues, these facts let you verify them without redoing the computation.
slides.explain: In our $2\times2$ example the eigenvalues $1$ and $3$ add up to $4$ and multiply to $3$, matching the trace $2+2$ and the determinant $2\cdot 2 - 1\cdot 1$. Use this as a quick sanity check on every computation.
slides.takeaway: Trace equals the sum, determinant equals the product.

slides.title: Checking with NumPy
slides.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, 1],
              [1, 2]])
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
print(vals)        # [3. 1.]
print(vecs[:, 0])  # [0.707 0.707]
explain: Build the matrix as a 2-D array.
`eig` returns the eigenvalues and a matrix whose **columns** are unit eigenvectors.
The eigenvalues we found by hand: 3 and 1.
Column 0 is $(1,1)/\sqrt 2$, our $\mathbf v$ scaled to length 1.
slides.about: The same computation done by a library. It returns the eigenvalues and a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors, scaled to length 1.

slides.title: Diagonalisable or not?

columns.heading: Diagonalisable
columns.text: Enough eigenvectors to form a basis of the whole space.

columns.heading: Defective
columns.text: Too few independent eigenvectors: some directions are missing.

slides.lead: Having $n$ independent eigenvectors is what makes everything easy. Not every matrix has them.
slides.explain: Diagonalisable matrices behave like diagonal ones in the right basis, which is why powers are easy. The shear is the standard warning: it has the eigenvalue $1$ twice, but only one line of eigenvectors, so the basis cannot be completed.

slides.question: A $2\times 2$ matrix has trace $5$ and determinant $6$. Its eigenvalues are
slides.explain: They must sum to the trace (5) and multiply to the determinant (6): only $2 + 3 = 5$, $2\cdot 3 = 6$.

slides.title: Remember
points: $A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v$, $\mathbf v \neq \mathbf 0$: directions that are only scaled.
Eigenvalues solve $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$; eigenvectors solve $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf v = \mathbf 0$.
Trace = sum, determinant = product of the eigenvalues.
